2 Samuel 1.audience: David's lament for Saul and Jonathan was taught to the people of Judah and written in the book of Jasher (2 Samuel 1:18). Readers knew it as a song of Israel's history.

culture.title: Bringing a king's crown
culture.text: The Amalekite brings Saul's crown and bracelet to David, expecting a reward for news of the king's death and for the royal insignia.

culture.title: Anointed shields
culture.text: Leather shields were rubbed with oil to keep them supple and ready for battle (Isaiah 21:5). David laments Saul's shield lying "as though he had not been anointed."

culture.title: Do not tell it in Gath
culture.text: Gath and Ashkelon were Philistine cities. David does not want the Philistine women to celebrate Israel's defeat, as Israelite women had celebrated David's victories.

2 Samuel 2.audience: Hebron was the chief city of Judah, where Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob were buried. Readers would see David first reign there over Judah alone for seven and a half years (2 Samuel 2:11).

culture.title: Two kingdoms
culture.text: Abner makes Saul's son Ishbosheth king over the northern tribes at Mahanaim, east of the Jordan, while Judah follows David—an early sign of the north–south division.

culture.title: A contest at the pool
culture.text: Twelve young men from each side fight in single combat at the pool of Gibeon before the general battle—another form of champion warfare.

2 Samuel 3.audience: Readers knew David's sons born at Hebron, listed here (2 Samuel 3:2–5), including Amnon, Absalom, and Adonijah, whose stories follow later.

culture.title: Taking a king's concubine
culture.text: Taking a dead king's concubine could be read as a claim to his throne. Ishbosheth accuses Abner of this with Saul's concubine Rizpah; Absalom later does the same openly (2 Samuel 16:21–22).

culture.title: Blood vengeance
culture.text: Joab kills Abner in the gate of Hebron to avenge his brother Asahel. Hebron was a city of refuge (Joshua 20:7), where a killer should have had a hearing.

culture.title: Mourning rites
culture.text: David orders the people to tear their clothes and put on sackcloth, and he follows the bier and fasts until evening.

2 Samuel 4.audience: Mephibosheth, Jonathan's lame son, is introduced here (2 Samuel 4:4). Readers would remember him in David's kindness later (2 Samuel 9).

culture.title: Bringing an enemy's head
culture.text: Bringing the head of a slain enemy proved his death. The two captains expect a reward for Ishbosheth's head; David executes them instead.

culture.title: Rest at noon
culture.text: In the heat of the day people rested indoors, which allowed the killers to enter Ishbosheth's house unnoticed.

2 Samuel 5.audience: Jerusalem became the city of David and Israel's capital from this time. Readers knew Zion as the hill of David's stronghold (2 Samuel 5:7).

culture.title: A neutral capital
culture.text: Jerusalem was a Jebusite city that no tribe had held. It lay between Judah and Benjamin, and taking it gave David a capital not tied to either the north or the south.

culture.title: The gutter
culture.text: David's men enter by "the gutter," probably a water shaft. A tunnel system leading to the Gihon spring has been found beneath ancient Jerusalem.

culture.title: Cedar from Tyre
culture.text: Hiram of Tyre sends cedar wood, carpenters, and masons. Phoenicia was famous for cedar from Lebanon and skilled builders.

2 Samuel 6.audience: Readers knew the ark was carried by poles on the Levites' shoulders (Numbers 4:15; 7:9). Here it is carried on a new cart, as the Philistines had done.

culture.title: Dancing before the ark
culture.text: Processions with music and dancing were part of religious festivals. David dances wearing a linen ephod, a priestly garment.

culture.title: Gifts of food
culture.text: Kings marked great occasions by giving food to the people. David gives everyone a cake of bread, a portion of meat, and a flagon (a raisin cake).

2 Samuel 7.audience: Readers knew the house of David as the royal line that ruled Judah for about four hundred years. This chapter records God's promise that David's throne would be established forever (2 Samuel 7:16).

culture.title: House as palace, temple, and dynasty
culture.text: "House" can mean a building or a family line. David wants to build God a house (temple); God promises to build David a house (dynasty).

culture.title: Cedar houses
culture.text: Cedar was the most costly building timber. David lives in a house of cedar while the ark is in a tent.

2 Samuel 8.audience: This chapter summarizes David's wars against the Philistines, Moab, Zobah, Syria, Ammon, Amalek, and Edom. Readers knew these as the nations around Israel.

culture.title: Measuring captives with a line
culture.text: David makes the Moabites lie down and measures them with a line, putting two lines to death and keeping one line alive—a harsh practice of war.

culture.title: Royal officials
culture.text: The list of officials—commander, recorder, priests, scribe, and the Cherethites and Pelethites (a royal guard)—shows David's court taking shape like the courts of other kings.

2 Samuel 9.audience: Readers would recognize David keeping his covenant with Jonathan (1 Samuel 20:14–16) by caring for his son Mephibosheth.

culture.title: Eating at the king's table
culture.text: Eating at the king's table was a great honor and a provision for life. It also kept a possible rival from Saul's family close to the king.

culture.title: Restoring land
culture.text: David restores Saul's land to Mephibosheth, to be farmed by Ziba and his sons and servants.

2 Samuel 10.audience: The Ammonites lived east of the Jordan. Readers knew Rabbah, their capital, as the city David's army besieged in the next chapters.

culture.title: Shaving half the beard
culture.text: A full beard was a mark of dignity for men. Shaving off half and cutting the garments short was a deliberate public insult to David's messengers.

culture.title: Hiring mercenaries
culture.text: The Ammonites hire Syrian soldiers from Bethrehob, Zoba, Maacah, and Ishtob.

2 Samuel 11.audience: Readers knew Bathsheba as the mother of Solomon. Uriah the Hittite was one of David's mighty men (2 Samuel 23:39).

culture.title: When kings go to battle
culture.text: Spring, after the winter rains, was the season for military campaigns. David stays in Jerusalem while his army goes out.

culture.title: Rooftops
culture.text: Flat roofs were used for walking and resting in the cool of the evening. From the palace roof David could see into nearby courtyards.

culture.title: A soldier's abstinence
culture.text: Soldiers on campaign kept themselves from their wives (compare 1 Samuel 21:5). Uriah refuses to go home while the ark and the army are in tents.

2 Samuel 12.audience: Psalm 51 is titled as David's prayer when Nathan came to him after Bathsheba. Readers knew Solomon, born in this chapter, as David's successor.

culture.title: A parable
culture.text: Nathan tells a story about a rich man taking a poor man's only lamb. Prophets sometimes used such stories to lead a listener to judge himself.

culture.title: Fourfold restitution
culture.text: David says the rich man must restore the lamb fourfold, following the law for stolen sheep (Exodus 22:1).

culture.title: Fasting for the sick
culture.text: David fasts and lies on the ground while the child is ill, then washes and eats after his death—the reverse of ordinary mourning customs.

2 Samuel 13.audience: Readers knew Amnon as David's firstborn and Absalom as the son who would later revolt. Tamar is Absalom's full sister.

culture.title: Royal daughters' garments
culture.text: The king's unmarried daughters wore a distinctive long robe, described with the same phrase used for Joseph's coat (Genesis 37:3). Tamar tears hers in grief.

culture.title: Sheep-shearing feast
culture.text: Sheep-shearing was a time of feasting, and Absalom invites the king's sons to his shearers at Baalhazor.

culture.title: Fleeing to his grandfather
culture.text: Absalom flees to Talmai king of Geshur, his mother's father, and stays three years.

2 Samuel 14.audience: Tekoa was a town of Judah, later the home of the prophet Amos (Amos 1:1). Readers would see Joab use a woman from Tekoa to bring Absalom back.

culture.title: Appeals to the king
culture.text: Ordinary people could bring cases directly to the king. The woman's story of a son facing blood vengeance asks David to rule on a family matter.

culture.title: Absalom's hair
culture.text: Absalom cut his hair once a year, and it weighed two hundred shekels by the king's weight—a sign of vigor and beauty.

2 Samuel 15.audience: Readers knew the Mount of Olives, east of Jerusalem, and the brook Kidron below it. David crosses both as he flees the city.

culture.title: Winning hearts at the gate
culture.text: Absalom stands by the gate and promises justice to those with lawsuits, stealing the hearts of the men of Israel.

culture.title: Chariot and runners
culture.text: Absalom prepares chariots, horses, and fifty men to run before him—marks of royal status.

culture.title: Mourning on the ascent
culture.text: David climbs the Mount of Olives barefoot, with his head covered, weeping—signs of mourning.

2 Samuel 16.audience: Readers knew Shimei of Saul's family and his cursing of David; Solomon later deals with him (1 Kings 2:8–9, 36–46).

culture.title: Throwing stones and dust
culture.text: Shimei throws stones and dust at David as he walks along the hillside, a public act of contempt.

culture.title: A tent on the roof
culture.text: Absalom goes in to his father's concubines in a tent on the palace roof, in the sight of all Israel—a public claim to the throne.

2 Samuel 17.audience: Mahanaim, east of the Jordan, was where Ishbosheth had reigned. David now takes refuge there with the help of Barzillai and others from Gilead.

culture.title: Hiding in a well
culture.text: A woman hides David's messengers in a well and spreads grain over the cover to disguise it.

culture.title: Supplies for the king
culture.text: Shobi, Machir, and Barzillai bring beds, basins, pottery, wheat, barley, flour, parched grain, beans, lentils, honey, butter, sheep, and cheese for David's people.

culture.title: Ahithophel's death
culture.text: When his advice is rejected, Ahithophel goes home, sets his house in order, and hangs himself.

2 Samuel 18.audience: Readers knew this as the end of Absalom's rebellion and the grief of David, whose cry "O my son Absalom" was remembered (2 Samuel 18:33).

culture.title: Forest warfare
culture.text: The battle in the wood of Ephraim is described as more deadly than the sword, as rough, wooded terrain broke up Absalom's forces.

culture.title: Absalom's pillar
culture.text: Absalom had set up a pillar in the king's dale as a memorial because he had no son to keep his name. The text says it was called Absalom's place "unto this day."

culture.title: Runners with news
culture.text: A watchman on the gate could tell a runner by his stride. Messengers ran from the battlefield to bring the result.

2 Samuel 19.audience: Readers would see the tension between Judah and the northern tribes over who would bring the king back (2 Samuel 19:41–43), a rivalry that later split the kingdom.

culture.title: Unkept beard and feet
culture.text: Mephibosheth had not dressed his feet, trimmed his beard, or washed his clothes since David left—signs of mourning.

culture.title: Crossing the Jordan
culture.text: A ferry boat carries the king's household across the Jordan. The river's fords were the main crossing points.

culture.title: Too old for the court
culture.text: Barzillai, at eighty, declines life at court, saying he can no longer taste food or hear singers.

2 Samuel 20.audience: Abel of Bethmaachah was in the far north near Dan. Readers would see another revolt, by Sheba son of Bichri of Benjamin, crushed there.

culture.title: A wise woman of the city
culture.text: A wise woman negotiates with Joab from the wall. Towns valued such counselors; she says the city was known for its wise advice.

culture.title: Siege ramps
culture.text: Besiegers piled up an earth ramp (a "bank") against the city wall and battered it to break through.

2 Samuel 21.audience: Readers knew of Joshua's treaty with the Gibeonites (Joshua 9:15). This chapter records a famine attributed to Saul's breaking of it.

culture.title: Rizpah's vigil
culture.text: Rizpah guards her sons' bodies from birds and beasts from the beginning of harvest until rain came. Leaving bodies unburied was a great shame.

culture.title: Giants of Gath
culture.text: One of the Philistine giants had six fingers on each hand and six toes on each foot.

2 Samuel 22.audience: This song of David appears again, with small differences, as Psalm 18. Readers used it in worship.

culture.title: Rock, fortress, and horn
culture.text: David's images for God—rock, fortress, shield, horn, and high tower—are military terms for places and means of defense in the hill country.

culture.title: Feet like hinds' feet
culture.text: The hind (a female deer) moves surefootedly on steep rocky heights.

2 Samuel 23.audience: Readers would recognize the names of David's mighty men, including Uriah the Hittite, who closes the list (2 Samuel 23:39).

culture.title: Water from Bethlehem's well
culture.text: Three of David's men break through the Philistine garrison to bring him water from Bethlehem's well. David pours it out before the LORD as a drink offering instead of drinking it.

culture.title: Elite warriors
culture.text: Kings kept a band of elite warriors, ranked by their deeds. David's were known as the three and the thirty.

2 Samuel 24.audience: Readers knew the threshing floor of Araunah as the place where the temple was built (2 Chronicles 3:1). David buys it in this chapter.

culture.title: Counting the people
culture.text: Census-taking was tied to military strength and taxation. Joab objects to the king's command (2 Samuel 24:3).

culture.title: Buying, not taking
culture.text: David insists on paying for the threshing floor and oxen: "neither will I offer burnt offerings unto the LORD my God of that which doth cost me nothing."
